Bret Taylor has done almost everything in business and tech, from creating Google Maps to becoming Facebook's CTO to co-running Salesforce and now chairing OpenAI.

But there is one thing Taylor has never done, and which he says matters more than anything.

“I think the greatest achievement for an entrepreneur,” he told Reid Hoffman in 2024, “is to create a company and a brand that outlives you.”

Taylor’s first two startups, FriendFeed and Quip, were sold. Then shut down by their buyers.

His third and most recent business, Sierra, builds AI agents for large businesses to talk with their customers. He started it at 42 with his old friend Clay Bavor. Today, in a new announcement, it's being valued at over $30 billion, making Sierra the furthest Taylor has ever taken a company of his own.

So @domcooke called on Taylor at Sierra's office in San Francisco to ask whether it's easier or harder than ever to build a company that lasts, why every one of Taylor's co-founders has come from Google, and whether Sierra might complete his journey as an entrepreneur.

They also discussed his teenage years as a roadie for a ska band, how companies can differentiate in a world of agent-to-agent commerce, and how to make drinking cool again.

Enjoy this Q&A with one of the great elder statesmen of Silicon Valley, Bret Taylor.

@TimDraper almost missed Coinbase.

In his account, @brian_armstrong originally pitched Coinbase to Joel Yarmon and Tim. Draper liked Armstrong, but the firm had already invested in CoinLab, a Bitcoin exchange focused on institutional investors. They made a strategic judgment: Coinbase was going after retail consumers, and they thought that route would take too long. So Draper passed.

His son @AdamDraper saw it differently. Adam Draper met Brian separately and wrote Coinbase his first check. Then the market started answering the question.

Coinbase grew, consumer adoption accelerated. Crypto moved far beyond the relatively small audience that existed when the company was founded. And when Coinbase raised another round, Draper Associates invested. Tim writes that the Coinbase investment ultimately returned nearly twice the size of an entire Draper Associates fund.

There’s an important lesson buried in the part of the story where they were initially wrong. The team correctly recognized Brian Armstrong as exceptional, but underestimated the path he had chosen.

Why it matters for builders: investors can be wrong about your market timing, your customer, or even your entire strategy while still recognizing something unusual in you. And investors should remember the inverse: sometimes the unconventional go-to-market strategy is exactly what creates the enormous market.

Retail crypto looked like the longer road, yet it became the road to mass adoption.

Many reasons. Frustrated developers would write in system prompts 'If the user asks you to do X, don't ask questions, JUST DO IT!' But this increasingly became an issue in early 2025, which resulted in the really obsessively RL'd generation of models that arrived late that year.

That obsession with independent task completion, combined with the increase in capabilities and the increase in possible time spent on a task, ended up making people increasingly nervous when they saw what the models would get up to in internal tests. It turned into a Sorcerer's Apprentice story, basically. All of this is downstream of the obsession with training them to be superhuman at code. Which, despite its success, has been a disaster in many ways. We wouldn't be having these problems if we had trained them to be poets instead. Of course, this would have been slightly less marketable, which is why we are where we are.
